\chapter{Synthesis --- Asking Without Sounding Rude}
\label{ch:synthesis-commands}
\hlchaptermodality{132}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can pick the command form that matches my relationship to the listener.}

Complete ES-C50-sintesis-pedir-bien: command a friend and a stranger, and say where a Spanish command's politeness lives.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — asking without sounding rude}

\label{lesson:ES-C50-sintesis-pedir-bien}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}eat\textquotedblright{} to a friend. (\emph{Come}.) In English, saying \textquotedblleft{}Eat.\textquotedblright{} to somebody lands hard. You are about to learn that it does not land the same way here.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
English has almost no polite imperative. \emph{Eat.} \emph{Sit.} Bare, they sound like orders to a dog, so English speakers pad them: \emph{could you}, \emph{would you mind}.

Spanish needs no padding, because it spends its politeness elsewhere — \textbf{on the choice of person}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Come.} — to a friend. Perfectly warm. \emph{Coma, por favor.} — to a stranger. Perfectly polite.
\end{quote}

The \emph{tú} command is not blunt; it is \textbf{intimate}. Using it says \emph{we are on those terms}, which between friends is friendly rather than bossy. The \emph{usted} command is not cold; it is \textbf{respectful}, for the same reason.

So an English speaker's mistake here is not tone. It is picking the wrong person: \emph{usted} with a friend sounds stiff, \emph{tú} with a stranger presumptuous. \textbf{The politeness lives in the pronoun you chose before the command left your mouth.} \emph{Por favor} helps and costs nothing, but here it is a garnish rather than the structure.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{The exchange}
The same four things said twice — once to a friend, once to a stranger.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{To a friend:} \emph{Ven. Come. No hables. Ten.} \textbf{To a stranger:} \emph{Venga. Coma, por favor. No hable. Tenga.}
\end{quote}

Read both aloud. The first is not ruder; it is closer. Say the second to somebody you have known for years and you have not been polite — you have put a small distance between you, and they will hear it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ven\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Venga\textquotedblright{} — hear the distance, not the rudeness
  \item the friend row, then the stranger row, straight through
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{Come} rude to a friend? (\textbf{No} — it is \textbf{close}.) Where does the politeness of a Spanish command live? (In the \textbf{person you chose}.) And what does \emph{usted} with an old friend sound like? (\textbf{Distance}, not courtesy.)
\end{tcolorbox}
